policy: Worked engineering cases are synthetic teaching examples. They are source-governed and internally publication-authorized, but they are not independent human SME approval, measured production evidence, universal process recipes, validated production limits or machine-control authority.

sourceSeeds.title: Moldflow — Clamp force result
sourceSeeds.scope: Documents clamp force as the resultant of pressure acting over projected area in Moldflow analysis; tool/model assumptions and machine/tool-specific margins remain controlling.

sourceSeeds.title: Analysis of gate freeze-off time in injection molding
sourceSeeds.scope: Experimental study of gate/cavity geometry effects on gate solidification and pressure evolution. Numerical results are study-specific.

sourceSeeds.title: e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Experimental design
sourceSeeds.scope: Engineering experimental-design framework including main effects and interaction terms; does not supply injection-moulding production setpoints.

sourceSeeds.title: e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Process capability
sourceSeeds.scope: Definitions and assumptions for Cp/Cpk and capability interpretation, including stable-process and distribution/sample-size considerations.

sourceSeeds.title: Multiple In-Mold Sensors for Quality and Process Control in Injection Molding
sourceSeeds.scope: Experimental in-mould sensing work supporting cavity-pressure trace interpretation, sensor-position context and process/quality monitoring boundaries.

sourceSeeds.title: From Manual to Automated: Exploring the Evolution of Switchover Methods in Injection Molding Processes—A Review
sourceSeeds.scope: Review of filling-to-holding switchover methods; supports early/late switchover consequences and sensitivity to material, machine and environmental conditions without defining a universal transfer point.

cases.title: Clamp-force estimate: expose every assumption
cases.setup: Projected area is 120 cm². An engineering teaching study assumes a representative cavity pressure of 55 MPa only to illustrate the pressure × area relationship.
assumptions: Projected area includes only the stated synthetic part/runner area.
55 MPa is an assumed representative pressure for arithmetic teaching; it is not inferred from machine injection pressure.
No tool-specific preload, safety margin or machine-rating decision is included.
cases.interpretation: 660 kN is the arithmetic result of the stated assumptions. It is not automatically the required machine clamp rating.
boundaries: Real decisions require actual projected area, pressure distribution, cavity/feed-system contribution, mould support/stiffness, machine/mould limits and the site's engineering margin policy.
No automatic machine-control or production recipe authority is created.

claims.statement: Separating-force arithmetic can be illustrated as pressure × projected area when the assumed pressure and area are explicit; the result is an estimate, not automatically a machine clamp setting.

cases.title: Staged pressure-loss study: upstream pressure is not cavity pressure
cases.setup: At a controlled comparable fill condition, displayed upstream injection pressure is recorded while successive portions of a synthetic flow path are added.
calculationSteps: Apparent increments across the staged additions are 18 MPa, 16 MPa, 24 MPa and 14 MPa.
The largest synthetic increment occurs when the gate/early-cavity portion is added.
cases.interpretation: The sequence identifies where pressure demand appears to increase and therefore where to investigate. It does not prove that the gate is defective, and the displayed upstream signal must not be relabelled as cavity pressure.
boundaries: The comparison requires controlled comparable states and valid machine/sensor semantics.
A staged pressure signal is diagnostic evidence, not causal proof.

claims.statement: Successive flow-path restrictions can be compared through controlled pressure observations, but upstream machine pressure is not equivalent to local cavity pressure.

cases.title: Gate-seal study: find a response plateau, not a universal hold time
cases.setup: All selected conditions are held constant while hold duration changes and mean part mass is observed.
calculationSteps: 6 → 8 s change = +0.01 g
8 → 10 s change = +0.00 g at the shown resolution
cases.interpretation: The synthetic mass response approaches a plateau around the 6–8 s region. A real study needs repeated observations, measurement-resolution awareness and critical quality checks.
boundaries: The result is specific to material, gate, mould and thermal state.
The example does not establish a generic hold time.

claims.statement: A controlled hold-duration study may use a plateau in an appropriate part response as evidence of effective gate isolation for the studied system, but the result is not universal.

cases.title: Pressure-trace interpretation: peak alone can hide history
cases.setup: Two synthetic cavity-pressure traces both reach 60 MPa peak pressure, while their pressure-time areas differ.
calculationSteps: Relative area difference = (120 - 90) / 90 × 100 = 33.3%
cases.interpretation: Equal peak pressure does not make two traces equivalent. Transfer timing, packing duration, decay shape and pressure-time area may expose process-history differences.
boundaries: Sensor location, type, calibration, sampling and cavity identity remain part of the evidence.
A trace correlation does not automatically prove causality outside the studied process window.

claims.statement: Cavity-pressure interpretation can require trace features beyond peak value, with sensor placement and calibration retained as evidence context.

cases.title: Two-factor DOE: an interaction can reverse the apparent answer
cases.setup: Response is synthetic warpage in millimetres; lower is better for this teaching example only.
calculationSteps: At low mould temperature: high − low fill speed = 0.31 − 0.42 = -0.11 mm
At high mould temperature: high − low fill speed = 0.30 − 0.29 = +0.01 mm
cases.interpretation: The fill-speed effect changes with mould-temperature level, so a one-factor statement such as 'higher speed reduces warpage' would be misleading.
boundaries: Real conclusions require an appropriate design, replication/randomisation or blocking where needed, residual checks and confirmation runs.
Factor ranges must remain within safe and qualified limits.

claims.statement: Factor effects can depend on other factor levels; interaction terms are therefore part of factorial experimental reasoning.

cases.title: Multi-cavity variation: pooled data can hide a cavity problem
cases.setup: A synthetic four-cavity mass summary shows similar within-cavity spread but different cavity means.
calculationSteps: The four cavity means average to 12.015 g, approximately 12.02 g at two decimal places.
Opposite offsets in cavities 2 and 4 can be hidden by the pooled mean.
cases.interpretation: Retain cavity identity before pooling so systematic cavity bias is not disguised as ordinary overall variation.
boundaries: Do not infer capability from these summaries alone; specifications, stability, sampling design and measurement-system adequacy are missing.
Tooling changes require repeatable cavity-specific evidence.

claims.statement: Pooling cavity-specific observations can hide systematic cavity offsets; capability claims require additional process and measurement evidence.

cases.title: Capability example: good spread does not compensate for poor centring
cases.setup: Synthetic specification is 10.00 ± 0.20 mm, giving LSL 9.80 mm and USL 10.20 mm. Teaching estimates use mean 10.08 mm and s = 0.04 mm.
cases.interpretation: The synthetic spread is narrower than the tolerance width, but off-centre location lowers Cpk relative to Cp.
boundaries: Capability arithmetic is not trustworthy merely because it can be calculated; process stability, sampling, distribution assumptions where applicable and measurement-system adequacy must be established.
No customer/site acceptance threshold is inferred.

claims.statement: Cp describes specification width relative to process spread while Cpk also reflects centring; meaningful capability interpretation requires the method's assumptions and process context.

cases.title: Conditioning and dimensional state: define when a dimension is measured
cases.setup: A reinforced-polyamide teaching example measures 100.00 mm after a defined dry-state interval and 100.18 mm after a defined conditioning protocol.
calculationSteps: Absolute change = 100.18 - 100.00 = +0.18 mm
cases.interpretation: The example demonstrates why dimensional acceptance must define conditioning/time/environment and measurement method.
boundaries: It does not claim that a particular PA66-GF30 grade changes by 0.18%.
Real magnitude is grade-, geometry-, orientation- and conditioning-specific; current exact-grade supplier data remain controlling.

claims.statement: Dimensional comparisons require a defined conditioning and measurement state because polymer/environment history can affect measured dimensions.

cases.title: Cooling/heat-load estimate: useful arithmetic with explicit omissions
cases.setup: Synthetic moulded mass including runner is 0.080 kg, illustrative average specific heat is 1,800 J/(kg·K), and illustrative temperature drop is 180 K.
calculationSteps: Q = m × cp × ΔT
cases.interpretation: This is a simplified sensible-heat quantity, not a cooling-time formula.
boundaries: The estimate omits crystallisation/latent effects where relevant, mould/insert heat capacity, shear heating, losses outside the mould, spatial gradients and heat-transfer coefficients.
Real cooling design requires geometry-, material- and tool-specific analysis and measurement.

claims.statement: A sensible-heat estimate can illustrate energy scale when mass, specific heat and temperature change are explicit, but it is not by itself a cooling-time prediction.

cases.title: End-to-end diagnosis: short shot without reflex tuning
cases.setup: One cavity in a four-cavity mould becomes intermittently short while the other three remain full. Global machine actuals and shot mass are stable; the affected cavity also shows a colder local mould-surface measurement and a contaminated vent during an authorised inspection.
observations: Single-cavity defect pattern
Stable global machine actuals and shot mass
Colder local mould-surface measurement
Visible local vent contamination during authorised inspection
calculationSteps: Competing mechanisms: local thermal restriction; local vent restriction; gate/runner restriction; cavity-specific damage/obstruction; global delivery limitation.

Discriminating evidence: cavity identity, fill progression, local thermal evidence, vent condition, runner/gate comparison, actual-vs-commanded machine response and repeated post-intervention recovery.
cases.interpretation: Stable global delivery plus a repeatable single-cavity pattern weakens a global-machine hypothesis. It does not by itself prove that venting or temperature is causal.
boundaries: Any intervention must be safe and authorised.
A mechanism is promoted only after discriminating evidence and repeatable recovery; troubleshooting remains hypothesis-and-evidence based.

claims.statement: Cavity-specific defect patterns can be used to discriminate local from global hypotheses, but repeated recovery evidence is required before promoting a mechanism as causal.

cases.title: V/P transfer comparison: separate timing from pressure outcome
cases.setup: Three synthetic runs use the same material, tool and nominal fill profile while transfer position is shifted. The values teach comparison logic only.
calculationSteps: A→B end-of-fill cavity-pressure change = +7 MPa.
B→C end-of-fill cavity-pressure change = +6 MPa.
The pressure response changes progressively across the synthetic transfer shift, but the table alone does not identify the best transfer point.
cases.interpretation: Transfer timing changes the handover between velocity-controlled filling and pressure-controlled packing. Judge the transition with fill progression, actual machine response, cavity pressure and part-quality evidence rather than a position number alone.
boundaries: The positions and pressures are synthetic and are not machine settings.
A safe process window, machine response semantics, mould filling pattern and quality criteria remain controlling.

claims.statement: Velocity-to-pressure transfer should be interpreted as a process transition using actual filling/pressure/quality evidence rather than a universal position value.

cases.title: Feed-system balance: compare branches before blaming the cavity
cases.setup: A two-branch synthetic runner study records comparable upstream-to-cavity pressure demand and mean part mass for each branch.
calculationSteps: Pressure-demand difference B − A = 9 MPa.
Mean-mass difference A − B = 0.24 g.
cases.interpretation: The branch with higher synthetic pressure demand also produces lower mass, which is evidence to inspect runner/gate geometry, thermal state and cavity-specific restrictions. It is not proof of a single geometric cause.
boundaries: Keep material, fill-rate and thermal state comparable before interpreting branch differences.
Runner or gate modification requires authorised tooling engineering; the arithmetic is diagnostic, not a sizing prescription.

claims.statement: Controlled branch-by-branch pressure and quality comparisons can expose feed-system imbalance without assuming a specific restriction is causal.

cases.title: Venting diagnosis: defect location plus controlled recovery
cases.setup: A synthetic end-of-fill burn appears on one cavity while global machine actuals remain stable. An authorised inspection finds visible vent contamination.
calculationSteps: Observed burn count changes from 8/10 to 1/10 shots after the controlled intervention.
Global shot-mass stability is retained as evidence against a large global-delivery change.
cases.interpretation: The repeatable local pattern, inspection evidence and post-cleaning recovery strengthen a vent-restriction hypothesis, but thermal degradation and other mechanisms still require exclusion where evidence points that way.
boundaries: Never alter vents, guarding or mould steel without tooling authority and machine/site safety controls.
One recovery sequence is useful evidence; repeated production-relevant confirmation is required before promoting a causal conclusion.

claims.statement: Local defect location, authorised vent inspection and repeatable controlled recovery can strengthen a vent-restriction diagnosis without turning the symptom into automatic causal proof.

cases.title: Ejection trend: rising force is an investigation trigger
cases.setup: A synthetic production sequence shows increasing normalised ejector-current peak while part geometry and commanded ejection motion are unchanged.
calculationSteps: Latest − baseline current-peak change = +34 percentage points.
The mechanical/electrical trend and surface evidence move together in the synthetic sequence.
cases.interpretation: The trend justifies checking cooling state, draft/release condition, contamination, surface damage, alignment and ejector mechanism condition. It does not prove inadequate draft.
boundaries: Current/force semantics are machine specific and require the manufacturer documentation.
Tool access, lubrication, polishing or mechanical adjustment requires authorised maintenance/tooling procedures.

claims.statement: A repeatable rise in ejection load combined with part-surface evidence is a diagnostic trigger, not standalone proof of a particular mould-design fault.

cases.title: Valve-gate timing: preserve cavity-specific actual evidence
cases.setup: A synthetic two-cavity valve-gate sequence compares commanded opening offset with cavity-pressure rise and part mass.
calculationSteps: Mean-mass difference = 18.04 − 17.82 = 0.22 g.
The synthetic pressure-rise delay approximately follows the commanded opening offset, but actuator actuals are not supplied.
cases.interpretation: Command, actual valve motion, local pressure response and cavity quality should be aligned before concluding that timing caused an imbalance.
boundaries: Displayed zone temperature or valve command does not prove nozzle-tip melt state or actual pin motion.
Hot-runner servicing and timing limits remain controller/tool-manufacturer specific.

claims.statement: Valve-gate diagnosis should align command/actual timing with cavity-specific pressure and quality evidence instead of relying on command values alone.

cases.title: Fill study: preserve progression, not just the final short shot
cases.setup: A synthetic fill study records filled mass fraction at controlled progressive shot volumes with packing influence intentionally excluded from the teaching comparison.
calculationSteps: Progression increments are +23, +25 and +19 percentage points.
The smaller final increment is an observation to investigate, not proof of freeze-off or vent restriction.
cases.interpretation: A controlled fill progression helps localise where resistance or imbalance develops and gives context for weld lines, air traps and orientation. The final pattern must be interpreted with thermal, pressure and geometry evidence.
boundaries: The study is synthetic; actual fill-study procedures must stay within safe machine/mould/material limits.
Do not disable safety systems or use unapproved machine states to create a short shot.

claims.statement: Controlled progressive filling can reveal flow-front development and localise diagnostic questions, but a short-shot pattern alone does not prove a mechanism.

cases.title: Shot utilisation: arithmetic is not a machine-limit decision
cases.setup: A synthetic machine has a stated maximum shot mass of 300 g for the reference condition and a moulded shot mass of 180 g including the runner.
calculationSteps: Simple reference utilisation = 180 / 300 × 100 = 60%.
The 60% result is only a ratio of the two stated masses.
cases.interpretation: Shot-utilisation arithmetic can flag whether a process deserves review, but real usable shot capacity depends on material density, plasticising performance, residence history, screw geometry, machine documentation and the actual process.
boundaries: Do not convert this example into a universal preferred utilisation percentage.
Use the actual machine manufacturer specification and material/mould/process evidence for capacity and residence decisions.

claims.statement: A simple shot-mass ratio can be calculated when its basis is explicit, but it is not by itself a safe machine-capacity or residence-time criterion.

cases.title: Process window: seek a robust region, not a single magic point
cases.setup: A synthetic 3×3 study classifies acceptable appearance/dimension response across fill-rate and mould-temperature levels. Values are coded Low, Mid and High rather than production settings.
calculationSteps: The centre column is acceptable at all three synthetic fill-rate levels.
No single corner condition is robust across the synthetic matrix.
cases.interpretation: A process-window study looks for regions where requirements remain satisfied despite realistic variation. Confirmation requires quantitative quality criteria, stability, measurement adequacy and appropriate experimental design.
boundaries: Categorical labels are synthetic and do not define acceptable production limits.
Factor ranges must be safe, qualified and consistent with machine, mould and material documentation.

claims.statement: Process-window development should seek a confirmed robust region across relevant factors rather than infer universal optimum settings from one condition.

cases.title: Warpage diagnosis: use direction, cavity and time to discriminate
cases.setup: A synthetic flat moulding shows 1.2 mm bow immediately after ejection. After 24 h at the defined conditioning state, bow is 1.8 mm. Cavity 1 averages 1.8 mm while cavity 2 averages 0.7 mm.
observations: Warpage increases after ejection rather than remaining constant.
The two cavities show a persistent offset under the same nominal machine cycle.
The direction of bow is repeatable relative to part geometry.
assumptions: Measurement datum, fixture and conditioning state are held constant.
The values are synthetic and illustrate diagnostic reasoning only.
calculationSteps: Post-mould change = 1.8 - 1.2 = 0.6 mm.
Cavity mean difference = 1.8 - 0.7 = 1.1 mm.
cases.interpretation: The time trend supports a post-mould dimensional-development contribution, while the cavity offset supports a local mould/thermal/flow contribution. Neither observation alone proves one root cause; the next tests should discriminate thermal balance, orientation/packing and measurement effects.
boundaries: Do not convert these synthetic magnitudes into acceptance limits.
Tooling or process changes require product, material, mould and site authority.

claims.statement: Warpage diagnosis can use controlled time trends, direction and cavity pattern as discriminating evidence while preserving multiple plausible mechanisms.

cases.title: Weld-line diagnosis: appearance is not the same as structural performance
cases.setup: A synthetic moulding has a visible line downstream of a hole. The line is present in both accepted and rejected samples, while a product-specific strength test differs.
observations: The interface location follows the split-and-rejoin flow path around the hole.
Visual severity and measured strength do not rank samples in exactly the same order.
Vent condition and local front-arrival state remain candidate contributors.
assumptions: The product-specific test is defined by the controlling quality requirement.
No generic temperature or speed change is treated as an approved remedy.
calculationSteps: Classify the evidence into geometry-fixed observations, process-sensitive observations and product-performance measurements.
Select a test whose predicted result differs between gas/venting, thermal/front-condition and material-history hypotheses.
cases.interpretation: The visible line establishes the interface location but not the product consequence or root cause. Geometry, local flow-front condition, gas evacuation and material state must be considered together.
boundaries: The case does not define an allowable weld-line strength.
Process and tooling changes remain within supplier, mould and site limits.

claims.statement: A visible weld line should be evaluated against the actual product requirement and competing flow, gas, material and geometry mechanisms rather than by appearance alone.

cases.title: Splay investigation: follow the defect across material and machine boundaries
cases.setup: Silver streaking appears after a material container change. It is present in all cavities on Machine A, disappears when a verified-dry sample is introduced, and does not reproduce with the original suspect material after a later handling correction.
observations: The symptom initially follows a material-handling event rather than one cavity.
All cavities respond together.
A controlled material-condition change alters the symptom.
assumptions: The material identity is confirmed and drying/handling follows current supplier documentation.
The example does not claim that all silver streaks are moisture-related.
calculationSteps: Use the boundary pattern to rank common upstream mechanisms ahead of cavity-local mechanisms.
Repeat the comparison to test whether the symptom follows measured material condition rather than the first successful adjustment.
cases.interpretation: The evidence strengthens a material-condition hypothesis but still requires credible moisture/handling records and exclusion of other volatile or air-entrainment mechanisms.
boundaries: Supplier grade instructions control drying conditions.
A successful drying-related change is evidence, not universal proof that every future splay event has the same cause.

claims.statement: Material-, cavity- and machine-boundary patterns can help discriminate splay mechanisms, but moisture must be confirmed with material-specific evidence rather than assumed from appearance.

cases.title: Dimensional conditioning: define when the measurement exists
cases.setup: A synthetic critical dimension measures 50.08 mm at 30 min after moulding, 50.03 mm at 24 h and 50.02 mm at 72 h under a defined conditioning environment.
observations: The measured dimension changes with elapsed conditioning time.
The largest change occurs before the final observation interval.
assumptions: The same measurement method, datum and environment are used.
The synthetic values are not a product tolerance.
calculationSteps: 30 min → 24 h change = -0.05 mm.
24 h → 72 h change = -0.01 mm.
cases.interpretation: A process comparison made at inconsistent measurement times could confuse conditioning response with process change. The measurement reference condition must be part of the engineering result.
boundaries: Actual conditioning requirements follow the applicable material/product standard and quality plan.
The plateau-like trend does not prove that every material has stabilised by 72 h.

claims.statement: Dimensional comparisons require a defined measurement and conditioning reference because post-mould dimensions can change with time and environment.

cases.title: Monitoring alarm: a signal excursion is a trigger, not a root cause
cases.setup: A synthetic cavity-pressure feature has a stable baseline of 42–46 MPa over the studied window. One cycle records 51 MPa while the measured part characteristic remains within specification.
observations: The monitored feature is outside the established study window for one cycle.
The product measurement remains acceptable for that sampled part.
The next three cycles return to the prior signal range.
assumptions: Sensor identity, calibration and sampling configuration are unchanged.
The alarm threshold is a study-specific monitoring rule, not a universal production limit.
calculationSteps: Flag the excursion for investigation rather than automatically declaring product failure or root cause.
Compare the event with other process signals, cavity identity and subsequent recurrence before escalating the hypothesis.
cases.interpretation: A process alarm is evidence that the process differed from its monitored baseline. Product disposition and root-cause conclusions require the quality plan and corroborating evidence.
boundaries: Real alarm actions must be predefined by the site's quality/control plan.
This example does not authorize automated machine-control changes.

claims.statement: A monitored process excursion can justify investigation without itself proving product nonconformance or root cause.

cases.title: Black-speck source map: use cavity and chronology before repeated purging
cases.setup: Synthetic black specks occur in all cavities immediately after a long interruption, diminish over ten cycles, then disappear. On another run they occur only in cavity 4 and persist.
observations: The first pattern is time-linked and common to all cavities.
The second pattern is cavity-specific and persistent.
Both symptoms look visually similar.
assumptions: Approved machine/material procedures govern any purge, inspection or disassembly.
No intervention is performed solely from this conceptual example.
calculationSteps: Pattern A prioritises common upstream residence/degradation or contamination mechanisms.
Pattern B prioritises a local downstream/hot-runner/cavity-path mechanism before assuming the same upstream cause.
cases.interpretation: Chronology and cavity distribution can make the source search more efficient and reduce repeated corrective actions that do not test the suspected location.
boundaries: Appearance alone cannot distinguish contamination from degradation.
Hot polymer, nozzle, barrel and hot-runner work requires approved supplier/site safety procedures.

claims.statement: Time and cavity patterns can help localise plausible black-speck sources while preserving uncertainty between contamination and degradation mechanisms.

cases.title: Capstone investigation: competing causes after a maintenance change
cases.setup: A synthetic four-cavity part develops a 0.20–0.28 mm dimensional shift after planned mould maintenance and a material-lot change on the same shift. Cavity 3 moves most; the other cavities move less. Machine setpoints are unchanged.
observations: The dimensional shift begins on the first production run after maintenance and the material-lot change.
Cavity 3 shows the largest offset, while all cavities show a smaller common shift.
The measurement system repeats within the established study tolerance when the same conditioned parts are remeasured.
Coolant flow on the circuit nearest cavity 3 is lower than its previous documented baseline, while common machine-side pressure traces remain close to the prior baseline.
A retained sample from the previous material lot, processed after thermal stabilisation, reduces the common shift but does not remove the cavity-3 offset.
assumptions: All observations and values are synthetic teaching data.
Any cooling-circuit inspection or maintenance follows approved mould/site procedures.
The example does not establish product disposition, a universal tolerance, or a production setpoint.
calculationSteps: Separate the pattern into a common shift affecting all cavities and an additional cavity-3-specific offset.
Retain at least three live hypotheses: material-condition/lot contribution to the common shift, local cooling or tooling contribution near cavity 3, and a measurement/conditioning explanation.
Use the repeat measurement and retained-lot comparison to reduce confidence in a measurement-only explanation while preserving uncertainty about material versus thermal/tooling contribution.
Treat the low local coolant-flow evidence as support for a cavity-local thermal hypothesis, not proof; require recovery of the hydraulic/thermal evidence and part response before claiming correction.
cases.interpretation: The evidence supports a mixed-mechanism model more strongly than any single-cause story: the retained-lot comparison suggests a material-related contribution to the common shift, while the persistent cavity-3 offset and local cooling evidence support an additional cavity-local mechanism. The investigation should preserve both until controlled recovery evidence separates them.
boundaries: A successful process adjustment that masks the dimensional shift would be containment evidence, not automatic root-cause proof.
Tooling or cooling intervention requires approved maintenance authority and post-intervention verification.
Product acceptance and disposition remain governed by the applicable quality plan and measurement requirements.
No automated machine-control or universal process recipe authority is created.

claims.statement: A complex moulding problem can require more than one active mechanism; cavity, chronology, retained-material, measurement and system-response evidence can be combined to update competing hypotheses without forcing premature single-cause certainty.

cases.title: Filling-boundary diagnosis: local flash without reflex clamp adjustment
cases.setup: A synthetic four-cavity mould produces a thin flash at the same shutoff feature in cavity 2 while cavities 1, 3 and 4 remain clean. The flash appears after thermal stabilisation. Global machine actuals and part masses remain similar to the established baseline, and an authorised visual inspection later finds contamination at the cavity-2 shutoff.
observations: The defect is repeatably cavity-specific and location-specific.
The other cavities remain free of flash under the same global machine cycle.
Global machine actuals and overall part-mass pattern remain close to the prior baseline.
The symptom appears at a defined shutoff feature after the mould reaches a stable thermal condition.
Authorised inspection identifies contamination at the affected local shutoff.
assumptions: All observations are synthetic teaching data.
The example assumes no machine or mould limit is exceeded and creates no instruction to increase clamp force or reduce viscosity.
Any shutoff inspection or cleaning follows approved mould and site procedures.
calculationSteps: Start with at least three plausible mechanisms: a local shutoff gap/contamination condition, a cavity-local pressure/thermal contribution, and a global clamp or pressure condition.
Use cavity distribution to weaken a purely global explanation: one cavity at one feature behaves differently while the other cavities share the same global machine cycle.
Use the authorised inspection result as supporting evidence for the local shutoff hypothesis, but require repeatable post-intervention recovery before promoting it as causal.
If the flash persists after the local condition is restored, reopen the pressure, thermal, alignment and tooling hypotheses instead of compensating blindly with a global setting.
cases.interpretation: The cavity-specific boundary and local shutoff evidence make a local tooling/contamination mechanism more plausible than a global clamp-force explanation. The evidence is not complete until the local condition is corrected under approved procedure and the flash response is shown to recover repeatably without creating a new defect.
boundaries: Do not increase clamp force, pressure or temperature from this example; machine, mould, material and site limits remain controlling.
Containment or temporary symptom reduction is not automatic root-cause proof.
Physical inspection, cleaning or tooling work requires approved maintenance authority.
Product acceptance remains governed by the applicable quality plan.

claims.statement: A repeatable cavity- and feature-specific flash pattern can be used to prioritise local tooling or shutoff hypotheses over purely global explanations, but repeatable recovery evidence is required before promoting the local mechanism as causal.

humanReviewScope.required: All 26 worked cases are attached to chapters inside the 46-chapter independent human SME scope; each case requires arithmetic/reasoning, assumptions, evidence fit, synthetic-data labelling and non-universal-boundary review.
